## The data structure

The raw DIA mass spectrometry data was processed using DIA-NN, which outputs a report file in `.parquet` format.
Unlike a simple abundance matrix, this is a **long-format** table --- each row corresponds to a single precursor--sample combination, rather than one row per precursor across all samples simultaneously.
The file contains precursor-level identifications and quantities for every sample, along with quality metrics from the DIA-NN search.

We read this file into R using the `read_parquet` function from the `arrow` package.

```{r}
#| label: read-diann-data
diann_df <- read_parquet("data/monkeypox_plasma_proteomes.parquet")
```

We can inspect the dimensions and column names to understand what the data contains.

```{r}
#| label: examine-data-structure
dim(diann_df)
names(diann_df)
```

The key columns we will use in our analysis are:

- **`Precursor.Id`**: a unique identifier for each precursor --- typically the modified peptide sequence and charge state (e.g. `"PEPTM[ox]IDEQ..2"`)
- **`Protein.Group`**: the canonical protein group identifier used for aggregation to protein level.
  Proteins that cannot be distinguished from each other based on proteotypic peptides detected in the data are grouped together under one Protein Group.
- **`Protein.Ids`**: every UniProt accession the precursor matches, before protein inference
- **`Genes`**: the gene symbol(s) associated with the identified proteins
- **`Run`**: the identifier for the sample run --- one value per LC-MS sample injection
- **`Precursor.Normalised`**: the quantified abundance of the precursor in that run, after DIA-NN's cross-run normalisation (described below)
- **`Precursor.Quantity`**: the same abundance before normalisation
- **`Normalisation.Factor`**: the factor DIA-NN multiplied `Precursor.Quantity` by to give `Precursor.Normalised`
- **Q-value columns** (`Q.Value`, `PG.Q.Value`, `Lib.Q.Value`, `Lib.PG.Q.Value` and others): the estimated false discovery rates for each identification, described in the DIA-NN Q-value callout in lesson 01

The report also contains chromatographic quality metrics per precursor per run.
For example:

- **`FWHM`**: Full-Width at Half Maximum of the chromatographic peak, a measure of peak shape quality --- narrow, symmetrical peaks are preferred

We will use the Q-value columns to filter the data in the next lesson.

We will be using the `QFeatures` Bioconductor package to import, store, and manipulate our data.
Before we import the data it is first necessary to understand the structure of a `QFeatures` object and its underlying `SummarizedExperiment` objects.

{{< include ../_shared/_qfeatures_structure.md >}}

The best way to get our head around the `QFeatures` infrastructure is to import our data into a `QFeatures` object and start exploring.

## Importing sample metadata

Sample metadata is information related to each sample that helps us interpret, organise and analyse our proteomics data.
This data is something you must create yourself, related to your experiment.
You can use a spreadsheet program such as Excel, or it can be coded in R directly.

Here, we have created a sample metadata file in Excel.
This file is called `monkeypox_metadata.xlsx`.
It provides information about each sample, including which group (MPXV, COVID-19, or Control) each run belongs to.
We use the `read_excel` function from the `readxl` package to import the data into R.

```{r}
#| label: explore-assay-structure
sample_metadata <- read_excel("data/monkeypox_metadata.xlsx")
print(sample_metadata)
```

The file holds the `sample_id`, which is the name of each sample, together with its group, sex and age group.
The `runCol` column holds a concise, human-readable label for each sample.
`readQFeaturesFromDIANN` matches each run in the DIA-NN report to a row of the metadata through a column that must be called `runCol`.
In the next section we add the same `runCol` values to `diann_df`, so that the two can be matched.


{{< include ../_shared/_pipe.md >}}

### Cleaning run names

DIA-NN takes the names in the `Run` column from the raw data file names, so they often carry folder names, file extensions or other text that is not part of the sample name in the metadata.
In this dataset, acquired on a SCIEX instrument, each run name joins the name of the `.wiff2` folder with the name of the `.wiff.scan` file.
We need to clean up these run names so that they match the `sample_id` field in our metadata.

```{r}
#| label: parse-sample-metadata
# Clean Run names
diann_df[, "Run"] %>%
  unique() %>%
  head(2)

# DIANN has pasted the name of the .wiff2 folder as well as the .wiff.scan
# files together. So we need to clean up the Run names so that they match
# the metadata `sample_id` field.
diann_df <- diann_df %>%
  mutate(Run = sub('\\..*', '', Run))

# Check we have cleaned the Run names
diann_df[, "Run"] %>%
  unique() %>%
  head(2)
```

`merge` keeps only runs whose name appears in both tables, so a run whose name we failed to clean would be dropped without a message.
This check stops with an error instead.

```{r}
#| label: check-run-names-match
# Every run in the report must have a row in the metadata
stopifnot(all(unique(diann_df$Run) %in% sample_metadata$sample_id))
```

In the following code chunk we add a new column called `runCol` to the `diann_df` data.
This column will serve as a link between the metadata and the `diann_df` proteomics data as well as being useful for visualisation and annotating our data at a later stage in the analysis.

```{r}
#| label: view-column-data
diann_df <- diann_df %>%
  merge(
    sample_metadata[, c("sample_id", "runCol")],
    by.x = "Run",
    by.y = "sample_id"
  )
```

Each run name in `diann_df` now has its short `runCol` label alongside it.

```{r}
#| label: show-run-labels
diann_df %>%
  distinct(Run, runCol) %>%
  head()
```

## Normalisation in DIA-NN

Even when the same amount of material is intended to go into every run, technical factors make the measured abundances differ between runs.
For example, pipetting errors change the total amount injected, and other effects act differently on different peptides.
Normalisation removes these non-biological differences so that abundances can be compared between samples.

DIA-NN normalises the precursor quantities itself, once it has processed all the runs, and reports both versions: `Precursor.Quantity` before normalisation and `Precursor.Normalised` after it.
The [DIA-NN documentation](https://github.com/vdemichev/DiaNN) describes two modes:

- **Global normalisation** corrects for differences in the total amount of material injected into each run.
- **Retention-time-dependent normalisation**, the default, also corrects for effects that act differently on peptides according to their hydrophobicity, which is reflected in their retention time (RT).

For each precursor in each run, `Normalisation.Factor` records the factor that was applied.
If DIA-NN had applied only a global correction, every precursor in a run would share the same factor.
Plotting the factors against retention time for a few runs shows that this is not the case.

```{r}
#| label: plot-normalisation-factors
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
diann_df %>%
  filter(runCol %in% unique(runCol)[1:4]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RT, y = log2(Normalisation.Factor))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~runCol) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Retention time", y = "log2(Normalisation factor)")
```

Within each run the factor follows a curve along the retention time axis, and the shape of the curve differs between runs.
So DIA-NN has applied a different correction to each part of the chromatographic gradient.

We import `Precursor.Normalised` rather than normalising the data ourselves.
DIA-NN normalises at an earlier stage of the analysis, on individual precursors, where more information is available: it knows when each precursor eluted in each run.
After we aggregate to protein level, that information is lost, because the precursors of one protein elute at different times across the gradient.
A protein-level method, such as shifting each sample's median to a common value, can apply only one correction per sample.

::: {.callout-note}
#### When not to use the normalised quantities

Generic normalisation like this assumes that most peptides do not differ in abundance between samples, so that the differences remaining between runs are technical.
We make this assumption for these plasma samples, but it does not hold for every experiment.
For experiments such as protein fractionation, where many peptides are expected to differ between samples, the DIA-NN documentation suggests a custom normalisation.
This can be applied to `Precursor.Quantity`, or to data from DIA-NN run with normalisation disabled.
:::

## Reading into a `QFeatures` object

We use the `readQFeaturesFromDIANN` function to import the cleaned DIA-NN data into a `QFeatures` object.
This function creates one `SummarizedExperiment` per run, with each set containing the precursor-level quantification data for that run.
The `runCol` argument specifies which column in the input data frame identifies the run, and `quantCols` specifies the column of quantities to import, here `Precursor.Normalised`.

```{r}
#| label: explore-missing-values
dia_qf <-
  readQFeaturesFromDIANN(
    diann_df,
    quantCols = "Precursor.Normalised",
    fnames = "Precursor.Id",
    runCol = "runCol",
    colData = sample_metadata
  )
```

## Exploring the data

When we inspect our `QFeatures` object, we see that it contains 31 sets, each corresponding to a different sample run.
Each set contains the precursor-level quantification data for that run, with feature names given by the `Precursor.Id` column from the original DIA-NN output.

```{r}
#| label: extract-protein-names
dia_qf
```

By default if a `QFeatures` object has more than 6 samples, only the first three and last three sample summaries are printed to the screen.
To see all samples and their respective data summary, we can use the `experiments` function.

```{r}
#| label: count-unique-proteins
experiments(dia_qf)
```

We can quickly see how many precursors were measured per sample for example, we see for the first sample called `r names(dia_qf)[1]` there are `r nrow(dia_qf[[1]])` precursors.

We can access individual samples (sets, or `SummarizedExperiment`s) using standard double bracket nomenclature (this is how you would normally access items of a list in R).
As with all indexing we can use the list position or dataset name.

```{r}
#| label: examine-peptide-counts
dia_qf[[1]]
```

Is the same as,

```{r}
#| label: create-class-summary
dia_qf[["COVID_E1"]]
```

The quantitation data for each sample is stored in the `assay` container and can be extracted using the `assay` function.

```{r}
#| label: show-dimensions
assay(dia_qf[[1]]) %>%
  head()
```

::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

Why does `readQFeaturesFromDIANN` create one `SummarizedExperiment` per run, rather than a single combined set across all runs from the outset?
:::

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
The DIA-NN output contains per-run quality metrics stored in the `rowData` of each precursor.
These are run-specific values and would be ambiguous or impossible to retain if all runs were immediately merged into a single matrix.
By keeping one `SummarizedExperiment` per run, we can inspect and filter on these per-run metrics before joining the data.
We will join the per-sample sets into a single combined precursor set in the next lesson, once filtering is complete.
:::

### How many precursors per sample?

Each sample will have a different number of precursors identified and quantified.
We can explore this by inspecting the number of rows in each per-sample set, which corresponds to the number of precursors quantified in that sample.

::: {.callout-exercise}

   Use it to plot a histogram of precursor counts across samples.

2. Create a bar plot showing the number of precursors identified in each sample, coloured by group.
   Based on your plot:

- Which group tends to have the most precursors identified?
- Is there any sample that looks like an outlier?

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
**Task 1**

```{r}
#| label: access-metadata-slots
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 4

hist(nrows(dia_qf), xlab = "Precursors", main = "Precursor counts per sample")
```

**Task 2**

```{r}
#| label: create-subset
data.frame(
  n_precursors = nrows(dia_qf),
  sample = names(nrows(dia_qf))
) %>%
  merge(data.frame(colData(dia_qf)), by.x = "sample", by.y = "runCol") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample, y = n_precursors, fill = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Number of precursors") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_classic()
```
:::::
:::

### Exploring the row data

The `rowData` of each per-sample `SummarizedExperiment` contains quality metrics from DIA-NN.
This information can be accessed on a sample by sample level by using the `rowData` function.

```{r}
#| label: compare-sample-counts
rowData(dia_qf[[1]]) %>%
  head(2)
```

However, we want to access this information across all the samples.
To do this we can use the `rbindRowData` function.

```{r}
#| label: subset-multiple-features
rdata <- rbindRowData(dia_qf, i = names(dia_qf))
```

The `rbindRowData` functions returns a `DFrame` table that contains the row binded `rowData` tables from the selected assays.
In this context, `i` is a `character()`, `integer()` or `logical()` object for subsetting assays.
Only `rowData` variables that are common to all assays are kept.

Recall, there is also a slot in the `QFeatures` object that stores information on the samples.
This is the `colData` slot.

```{r}
#| label: compare-subset-counts
colData(dia_qf)
```

In the below code chunk we create a `data.frame` called `cdata` containing the sample information and merge this with the `rdata` so we get group information for each sample.
This will help with our data exploration.

```{r}
#| label: aggregate-features
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5

# 1. Create a data.frame of the sample information

cdata <- data.frame(colData(dia_qf))

# 2. Merge this with the row data
# Note: Our data is in separate sets, so the sample names are in the 'assay'
# column. We merge with the column data (using the runCol column) to get group
# information for each sample

rdata <- rdata %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  merge(cdata, by.x = "assay", by.y = "runCol")
```

Now we have one `data.frame` with precursor-level and sample-level information we can now visualise quality metrics from DIA-NN including the Full-Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of the chromatographic peaks.
In the code below we plot the distribution of FWHM values per sample, coloured by group.

```{r}
#| label: join-features
rdata %>%
  ggplot(aes(FWHM, group = Run, colour = group)) +
  geom_density() +
  theme_classic()
```

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Exploring rowData quality metrics

{{< level 2 >}}

The `rdata` object contains many columns from the DIA-NN `rowData` beyond FWHM.

1. Use `str(rdata)` to identify other numerical quality metric columns.
2. Choose one metric and create a plot to visualise its distribution across samples, coloured by group.
3. Do any metrics appear to differ systematically between groups, or between individual samples?
:::


```{r}
#| label: filter-by-fdr
#| include: false

save(dia_qf, file = "preprocessed/lesson02.rda")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

- DIA-NN outputs a `.parquet` format report file containing precursor- and protein-level quantification data for each sample
- DIA-NN normalises precursor quantities across runs using retention-time-dependent factors; we import these normalised quantities (`Precursor.Normalised`) because DIA-NN can correct each precursor according to its elution time, which a protein-level normalisation cannot
- The `readQFeaturesFromDIANN` function imports DIA-NN output into a `QFeatures` object, creating one `SummarizedExperiment` per sample run
- Sample metadata is stored in the `colData` of the `QFeatures` object and can be used to annotate samples with experimental group information
- The `rowData` of each per-sample `SummarizedExperiment` contains quality metrics from DIA-NN (e.g. FWHM, Q-values) that can be used to explore data quality and guide downstream filtering decisions
:::
